senses.gloss:
Āsuri
------------------------------------------
Among the षड्-दर्शनस् or the six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, Sāṅkhya-दर्शन has an important place. It is nearer to the Vedānta system and has been quite popular. Ideas of Sāṅkhya are found spread over the epics and the पुराणस् too.
The system is said to have originated from कपिल, and आसुरि was his chief disciple. Along with पञ्चशिख, the disciple of आसुरि, the three great teachers have put the system on a firm foundation. The Mahābhārata (12.219) gives an account of their teachings.
Nothing is known of आसुरि except that he was a teacher of Sāṅkhya, a disciple of कपिल and गुरु of पञ्चशिख. Mythological lores say that आसुरि was a होउसे-holder immersed in the world and it took a long time and much effort for his गुरु कपिल to awaken him to the path of spiritual life.
See also KAPILA, PAÑCAŚIKHA and SĀṄKHYA-DARŚANA.

aśuklākṛṣṇa
(‘that which is neither white nor black’)
------------------------------------------
This is a special term used by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his celebrated work the Yogasūtras (4.7). Normally the कर्म of individuals that fructify in this life or in the future lives is classified either as ‘śukla’ (‘white;’ i.e., पुण्य or meritorious) or as ‘kṛṣṇa’ (‘black;’ i.e., पाप or sinful). The former bring good results whereas the latter cause evil effects. But the karmas done by a perfected yogin are neither कृष्ण nor śukla, since he never commits sins; and offers the fruits of all his meritorious deeds to ईश्वर or God. Hence his कर्म is known as ‘aśukla-akṛṣṇa,’ ‘neither white nor black’ and does not produce any result that will bind him in any way.
See also KARMA.

asuras
(‘beneficent being,’ ‘those addicted to sense-pleasures’)
------------------------------------------
The metamorphosis of the meaning of the word ‘asura,’ from ‘beneficent god’ to ‘malevolent spirit or being’ in the Vedic and post-Vedic literature is rather baffling. In early Vedic literature (vide Ṛgveda 1.35.7; 1.131.1) the term denotes the Supreme Spirit. Derived probably from the root ‘as’ (‘to exist’), or ‘asu’ (‘prāṇa or life-force’), it must have originally meant the ‘Self-existent Being’ or the ‘Being of life-force and power.’ It is in this sense that the well-known Vedic deities इन्द्र and वरुण have been called ‘asuras’ (ibid 1.54.3; 1.24.14).
But soon the connotation changed. The Nirukta, the standard dictionary of Vedic terms, defines the ‘asuras’ as those ‘who are not satisfied in their positions,’ ‘the ever-fickle’ and ‘those who are deprived of their positions by the सुरस् or देवस्.’ In later literature, mostly the epics and the पुराणस्, they are posited as ‘a-सुरस्’ or ‘anti-gods,’ malevolent beings, ever opposed to the ‘suras’ or ‘devas,’ the ‘beings of goodness and light’. In this sense they are pictured as highly ambitious and aggressive people, rich, civilized and powerful, but ever bent on conquest and self-aggrandizement. And precisely because of this trait of theirs, they are ever in conflict with the देवस् representing the forces of goodness, refine-ment and culture.
Though conflicts between the देवस् and the असुरस् are legion, there have also been occasions when they have cooperated, as for instance, in the case of churning of the ocean to get अमृत or nectar. There have been great asura kings like प्रह्लाद, बलि, Śambara and बाण who were devotees of God (Viṣṇu or शिव).
In the mythological lore, the देवस् and the असुरस् are depicted as the children of the same ड़थेर्, the sage कश्यप, from his two wives अदिति and दिति. Sometimes, the असुरस् have been described as having been born out of the body of ब्रह्मा or प्रजापति, the Creator.
Whatever be the manner of their origin, the देवस् and the असुरस् appear more to be the archetypes of the good and the not-so-good beings in च्रेअतिओन्.
In the earlier religious literature, the दैत्यस् and the दानवस्, positively more malevolent beings, had been placed below the असुरस्. But gradually, the असुरस् were degraded and identified completely with the former.
One of the very special powers the असुरस् seemed to possess and excel in, was sorcery and magic.
Some Western scholars of Indology hazard the guess that the असुरस् were the hostile native rulers and tribes who were opposed to the आर्यन्स्. Due to lack of conclusive evidence to clinch the issue, it is difficult to accept such theories. The word may be more etymological and symbolical than historical, racial or social. It is significant to note that शङ्कर (8th cent. A. D.) the great philosopher mystic, defines the असुरस् as ‘those addicted to selfish bodily pleasures’ (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. 1.3.1)
See also DĀNAVAS, DAITYAS, RĀKṢASAS and SURAS.
